name: awk
description: A pattern-scanning and processing language: splits lines into fields and applies programs to them, ideal for column-based data.

flags.description: $1..$N are whitespace-separated fields; $0 is the whole line; NF is the field count.
Set the field separator (e.g. -F: for /etc/passwd, -F, for CSV).
Run the action only on lines matching the pattern.
Blocks that run before the first line and after the last.
Pass a shell variable into the awk program.

examples.explanation: Prints the first field (the client IP) of every log line.
Prints username and UID by splitting each line on colons.
Counts lines containing ERROR — a one-line log analyzer.
Skips the header row (NR>1) and prints the use-percent and mount point columns.
Field comparison: prints usernames whose UID is 1000 or higher (regular users on most distributions).

about: An awk program is a series of pattern {action} pairs evaluated per line. Default field separator is any run of spaces/tabs. Built-in variables: NR (line number), NF (fields in the line), FS/OFS (separators). awk also supports arithmetic, arrays, if/for — it is a full small language, which makes it perfect for quick reports without writing a script.
useCases: Extract and sum columns from logs and CSVs.
Reformat data between tools in a pipeline.
mistakes: Mixing up single and double quotes: the awk program must be in single quotes so the shell does not expand $1.
Forgetting -F when the separator is not whitespace, then wondering why $2 is empty.
distroNotes: gawk (GNU awk) adds features like PROCINFO and network access; mawk is a smaller, faster implementation common in minimal Debian installs; busybox awk is limited. Core syntax is portable across all of them.
